title: Speckle-based feedback control of optical dipole trap axial waist position
authors: D. A. Pershin, D. A. Kumpilov, A. E. Rudnev, G. E. Subbotin, A. M. Ibrahimov, I. S. Cojocaru, V. A. Khlebnikov, I. A. Pyrkh, P. A. Aksentsev, S. A. Kuzmin, A. D. Raskatov, A. K. Zykova, V. V. Tsyganok, A. V. Akimov
abstract: Cold neutral atoms is a powerful tool for many experiments ranging from frequency standards and sensing to quantum simulations. Sensitive experiments often demand transferring cold atoms from one vacuum chamber to the other with better optical access and vacuum. In case the transfer is done with a beam waist controlled by a focus-tunable lens, repeatability of the transfer as well as stability of the final position can be below the experimental demands. Here we implement the scheme for stabilization of the axial waist position of the optical dipole trap in the whole range of transfer (38 cm) using speckle patterns, which provides enough stability to achieve Bose-Einstein condensation of around 4*10^4 thulium atoms in the trap formed by the transport beam and the other beam in the target vacuum volume
summary: The researchers developed and implemented a speckle-based feedback control system to stabilize the axial waist position of an optical dipole trap during long-distance transport. By monitoring unique speckle patterns generated by the beam, they achieved stable trapping conditions necessary to successfully cool and condense tens of thousands of thulium atoms.
main_problem: The primary goal was achieving stable axial waist position control for an optical dipole trap (ODT) while transporting cold neutral atoms over a long distance.
main_result: Speckle-based feedback successfully stabilized the ODT beam waist over 38 cm, enabling subsequent Bose-Einstein condensation of approximately $4 	imes 10^4$ thulium atoms.
method: A novel feedback control loop was implemented using speckle patterns captured by a CMOS camera; the pattern's dot product with a reference set determined the necessary correction current to stabilize the trap waist.
model_or_system: The experiment utilizes cold neutral atoms (e.g., thulium) trapped in an ODT, which is manipulated using focus-tunable lenses and monitored via speckle patterns generated by coherent light scattering.
key_observables: Axial waist position ($w_p$), Center of Mass (CM) coordinate over time, number of condensed atoms vs. time, and the measured speckle pattern ($	ext{act}S$).
important_parameters: Transfer distance (38 cm), atom count ($\sim 4 	imes 10^4$ Th atoms), ODT potential depth ($U$), and feedback loop rate.
main_assumptions: The method bypasses the need for a perfectly known relationship between lens current and $w_p$; however, the analysis notes limitations regarding image acquisition time and computation speed.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the optical setup (Fig 1), the feedback mechanism using dot products and CM position tracking during potential changes (Fig 2), and the resulting BEC formation/thermal cloud evolution over time (Fig 3).
paper_structure: The paper details the physical scheme, derives the mathematical basis for speckle pattern measurement ($\sigma \propto w/h$), implements the feedback algorithm using dot products, validates stabilization through CM tracking, and concludes with successful atom condensation measurements.
why_interesting: This work provides a robust, non-invasive diagnostic tool (speckle imaging) to control critical parameters of optical traps in real-time, which is crucial for high-precision quantum simulations involving cold atoms.
